structure.title: I
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway reflecting on his father’s advice to reserve judgment, a principle that shaped his role as a confidant in college and later led to his disillusionment after returning from the East, except for Gatsby, whom he uniquely admires for his extraordinary capacity for hope. In the spring of 1922, Nick moves alone to West Egg, renting a modest eighty-dollar-a-month bungalow between two grand estates, and feels a renewed sense of purpose as he buys books on finance; after being asked for directions to West Egg village by a stranger, he gains a sense of belonging. He drives to East Egg to dine with his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, whom he knew at Yale, at their opulent Georgian Colonial mansion, where he meets Jordan Baker, who lies motionless on a couch throughout the evening. During dinner, Tom passionately endorses racial theories from The Rise of the Coloured Empires, Daisy casually declares she hopes her daughter will be a 'beautiful little fool,' and a telephone call reveals Tom’s affair in New York—a fact Jordan confirms to Nick in hushed tones; after another call silences the room, Daisy and Nick sit in twilight as she expresses disillusionment, though her sincerity is undercut by a smirk. Later, after Jordan reads aloud from the Saturday Evening Post and departs, Daisy and Tom teasingly question Nick about rumors of his engagement out West, which he denies. Returning to West Egg, Nick sits alone on an abandoned grass roller in his yard, observing the summer night until he sees Gatsby standing on his lawn, arms outstretched toward a distant green light at the end of a dock, trembling silently before vanishing into the shadows.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan from West Egg to New York, stopping at the desolate Valley of Ashes where they disembark to meet Tom’s mistress, Myrtle Wilson, at her husband George Wilson’s run-down garage; Tom insists Nick accompany them to New York, and they board separate train cars to avoid scrutiny. In New York, Myrtle buys a brown Airedale puppy for $10 from a street vendor, then takes a lavender taxicab to her cramped, gaudily furnished apartment on 158th Street, where she changes into a cream chiffon dress and transforms into a haughty socialite. The gathering escalates with the arrival of Myrtle’s sister Catherine and Mr. McKee, as heavy drinking, superficial conversation, and Myrtle’s recounting of meeting Tom on a train give way to chaos; Myrtle defiantly shouts Daisy’s name, provoking Tom to brutally break her nose with an open hand, leaving blood on the couch as women scramble to help and Mr. McKee wanders dazedly away. Overwhelmed, Nick departs with McKee in the elevator and later awakens exhausted on a bench at Pennsylvania Station, waiting for the 4 a.m. train, haunted by the night’s violence and artificiality.

structure.title: III
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway receiving a formal invitation to attend a lavish Saturday evening party at Jay Gatsby’s West Egg mansion, where guests arrive by car from New York—some in Rolls-Royces, others in station wagons—swarming the grounds with music, dancing, and excessive luxury under colored lights. While wandering among strangers and overhearing wild rumors that Gatsby killed a man or was a German spy, Nick Carraway meets Jordan Baker, who leads him to a library where a drunken guest with owl-eyed spectacles marvels at the authenticity of Gatsby’s real books; later, a fellow First Division veteran invites him to fly a hydroplane the next morning. Nick Carraway then encounters Gatsby himself, who reveals his identity after a conversation about the war and extends the hydroplane invitation, impressing Nick Carraway with his rare smile; Jordan reveals Gatsby claims to have attended Oxford, though she doubts it. As the party descends into chaos—with a drunken chorus girl weeping mascara-blackened tears, marital fights erupting, and a new coupe crashing into a ditch, leaving one wheel detached—Nick Carraway observes Gatsby standing alone on the porch bidding farewell as Owl Eyes claims he wasn’t driving and a dazed passenger emerges asking for a gas station. Nick Carraway later reflects on his daily life in New York: walking to the Probity Trust, dining with clerks, studying at the Yale Club, and nightly walks past the Murray Hill Hotel to Pennsylvania Station, while rekindling his acquaintance with Jordan Baker, whose dishonesty—cheating in a golf tournament and lying about damaging a car—fails to diminish his emotional detachment, as he grapples with ending a distant romantic engagement and concludes that he is one of the few honest people he knows.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning in July 1922, Gatsby’s West Egg mansion hosts a lavish party attended by dozens of guests from East Egg, West Egg, and New York, including the Chester Beckers, Leeches, Blackbucks, Dancies, Klipspringer, and others, many of whom spread wild rumors about Gatsby’s origins while engaging in bizarre personal dramas—such as Snell being run over by Mrs. Ulysses Swett’s automobile while drunk and Henry L. Palmetto’s suicide by subway—yet none know the truth about their host. Later that month, Gatsby arrives at Nick Carraway’s door in his cream-colored car with a three-noted horn, invites him to lunch, and during the drive to Manhattan, recounts an elaborate, contradictory biography claiming Oxford education, wartime heroism with a Montenegrin medal and an Oxford photograph as proof, while subtly hinting at hidden influence when he uses a white card to bypass a police stop. At noon in a cellar restaurant on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfshiem, a man with molar cuff buttons and nasal hair, who recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal and shockingly reveals he fixed the 1919 World Series; Gatsby abruptly leaves to make a phone call and vanishes when Nick Carraway tries to introduce him to Tom Buchanan. In a flashback to October 1917, Jordan Baker recalls meeting Daisy Fay in Louisville, seated in her white roadster with Lieutenant Jay Gatsby, whose intense gaze she never forgot; years later, after Daisy’s tumultuous courtship and marriage to Tom Buchanan—including a drunken attempt to return his three-hundred-fifty-thousand-dollar pearl necklace before the wedding—Nick Carraway learns from Jordan that Gatsby bought his mansion solely so Daisy could see the green light across the bay, and now seeks a quiet tea invitation to reunite with her, a request that moves Nick Carraway from curiosity to quiet fascination with Jordan herself as they ride through Central Park at twilight.

structure.title: V
structure.summary: On a quiet night in West Egg, Nick returns home to find Gatsby’s mansion illuminated at 2 a.m., silent except for the wind; Gatsby approaches him with invitations to Coney Island or a swim, which Nick declines. The next day, Nick agrees to arrange a tea with Daisy, and Gatsby, nervously avoiding appearing demanding, awkwardly offers Nick a confidential side business opportunity. On a rainy afternoon, Gatsby sends a gardener to cut Nick’s lawn and arrives in a white suit, visibly shaken; Daisy arrives by large open car with her chauffeur Ferdie, and their reunion is initially stifled by tension—Gatsby nearly knocks over a mantelpiece clock. After a painful silence, they relax, and Gatsby radiates joy as he invites Daisy to tour his mansion. They walk to the estate via the road and enter through the big postern, where Daisy marvels at its feudal silhouette, gardens, and floral scents. Inside, they encounter only Mr. Klipspringer in pajamas doing liver exercises; Gatsby displays his extensive collection of shirts, throwing them onto the table in a cascade of colors and monograms, which moves Daisy to stormy tears. Gatsby then points out the green light on Daisy’s dock, lamenting its diminished symbolic power, shows her photographs of Mr. Dan Cody and himself as a young man in yachting attire, and presents newspaper clippings about her. When Klipspringer is called to play piano, he performs two songs while Gatsby and Daisy sit in shadowed silence; as Nick prepares to leave, he notices Gatsby’s returning bewilderment but sees them reconnected through Daisy’s voice, utterly absorbed in each other and oblivious to his presence.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: A New York reporter arrives at Gatsby’s mansion one morning seeking a statement, inadvertently uncovering the origins of Gatsby’s notoriety, which had been fueled by wild rumors such as his secret boat-house and underground pipelines to Canada; the narrative then traces Gatsby’s transformation from James Gatz of North Dakota, who at seventeen rowed out to Dan Cody’s yacht on Lake Superior, began working for Cody aboard the Tuolomee in multiple roles over five years, and absorbed the habits and ideals of wealth—only to be cheated out of his $25,000 inheritance by Ella Kaye after Cody’s death, shaping his nightly reveries of grandeur and his self-constructed identity as a 'son of God' devoted to a 'vast, vulgar, and meretricious beauty.' Weeks later, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and is startled to find Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit arriving on horseback; Gatsby, visibly nervous and eager to please, insists they stay for drinks and supper, but their cold indifference and Mr. Sloane’s subtle exclusion force them to depart abruptly, leaving Gatsby standing alone. Later that week, Tom and Daisy attend one of Gatsby’s parties at twilight, where Daisy is captivated by the spectacle yet disturbed by its raw, unpolished energy, while Tom expresses open disdain; Gatsby watches her closely, hoping she will renounce Tom and return to their past, but after the party ends, he confides in Nick Carraway that she didn’t enjoy herself, insisting he can repeat the past and restore their lost love—refusing to accept that time has changed everything, and recalling the night they first kissed under moonlight.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On a broiling summer afternoon, Nick Carraway arrives by train at the Buchanans’ house to find Gatsby waiting, having dismissed his entire staff to avoid gossip over Daisy’s frequent visits; during a stifling lunch in the darkened dining room, Daisy openly declares her love for Gatsby, shocking Tom, who aggressively challenges Gatsby’s background and mocks his claim of being an Oxford man. The group drives in oppressive heat to Wilson’s garage in the Valley of Ashes, where a sick and desperate George Wilson reveals he plans to take Myrtle away, unaware she is having an affair with Tom; Myrtle, mistaking Jordan Baker for Tom’s wife, watches from the window in jealous terror as Doctor T. J. Eckleburg looms overhead. Later, the group retreats to a stifling suite at the Plaza Hotel in New York City, where Tom accuses Gatsby of bootlegging through Meyer Wolfsheim, and Gatsby demands Daisy admit she never loved Tom — but she breaks down, confessing she once loved Tom and still loves Gatsby, shattering Gatsby’s illusion. Tom orders Daisy and Gatsby to return to Long Island in Gatsby’s car, isolating them from the others. That evening, Myrtle Wilson rushes out of her upstairs room in Wilson’s garage and is struck and killed by a speeding yellow car that flees the scene; Michaelis and a witness describe the car as large and yellow, traveling at 50-60 mph. Tom and Nick arrive at the garage to find Wilson hysterical, crying 'Oh, my Ga-od!', and Tom insists he was driving a blue coupé from New York all afternoon, establishing an alibi before fleeing the scene in distress. Later, Nick leaves the Buchanan mansion and finds Gatsby waiting alone in the shadows, who confesses Daisy was driving the car that killed Myrtle but he will take the blame; through a pantry window, Nick observes Tom and Daisy sitting quietly together at the kitchen table, sharing food and ale with intimate calm, having already reconciled. Gatsby refuses to leave his post, standing vigil in the moonlight as Nick departs, guarding nothing but an illusion.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: On the dawn after a sleepless night haunted by a foghorn, Nick Carraway rushes to Gatsby’s mansion upon hearing a taxi arrive, finding Gatsby dejected after Daisy briefly appeared at her window then turned off the light. Together, they wander through the dusty, musty mansion, accidentally disturbing a ghostly piano, as Nick Carraway urges Gatsby to flee to Atlantic City or Montreal to avoid being traced by Daisy’s car—Gatsby refuses, clinging to the hope that she will choose him. In a vulnerable moment, Gatsby recounts his youth with Dan Cody and how he first fell in love with Daisy, misleading her into believing he had wealth and status despite being penniless. On the final afternoon before his departure, Gatsby sits silently with Daisy in a firelit room, savoring their emotional intimacy through subtle gestures, knowing they must part. After returning from the war and mistakenly being sent to Oxford, Gatsby learned of Daisy’s marriage to Tom Buchanan while still abroad; devastated, he traveled penniless by day-coach to Louisville, walking the streets where they once met, reaching desperately for the fading memory of her as the train pulled away. At dawn on Long Island, Gatsby declares Daisy never truly loved Tom, calling her reaction 'just personal,' and reveals he has never used his pool all summer; Nick Carraway, refusing to leave, misses two trains before shouting that Gatsby is worth more than Tom and Daisy’s 'rotten crowd,' to which Gatsby responds with a radiant, understanding smile. Meanwhile, George Wilson, shattered by Myrtle’s death and convinced the yellow car’s driver murdered her, becomes fixated on the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, declaring 'God sees everything.' After wandering for hours, Wilson arrives in West Egg and asks for Gatsby’s house. That afternoon, Gatsby, wearing his bathing suit and instructing the butler to relay any calls to him at the pool, floats on a pneumatic mattress—no call comes, signaling his lost hope—and is shot dead by Wilson, who then kills himself; Nick Carraway arrives to find Gatsby’s body in the pool and Wilson’s corpse in the grass, completing the tragedy.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: Following Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is overwhelmed by the intrusion of police, photographers, and reporters at Gatsby’s mansion, where children sneak in to stare at the pool; sensationalized media reports label Wilson a 'madman' and Catherine denies any connection between Myrtle and Gatsby, shielding Daisy and Tom from blame. Nick Carraway desperately tries to reach Daisy and Meyer Wolfshiem by phone and later sends a letter to Wolfshiem’s Broadway office, receiving only a cold, evasive reply citing business obligations, while a mistaken long-distance call from Chicago about a bond scandal is abruptly cut short when Nick Carraway reveals Gatsby is dead. On the third day, Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, visibly frail and bundled in a cheap ulster, and is shown his son’s body and cherished possessions—including a photograph of the mansion and a worn copy of Hopalong Cassidy with Gatsby’s childhood self-improvement schedule—revealing his profound pride in his son’s ambition. Only a handful of people attend the funeral: Gatz, Nick Carraway, the Lutheran minister from Flushing, four or five servants, the West Egg postman, and the mysterious owl-eyed man who appears unexpectedly in the rain to say 'Amen to that' after a murmured quote about the blessed dead; Klipspringer calls to request his tennis shoes and declines attendance, while Wolfshiem refuses to come, citing a personal rule against involvement after death. Nick Carraway later encounters Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, who defensively admits he told Wilson Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as necessary; Nick realizes Tom and Daisy are careless people who destroy lives and retreat behind wealth. After packing and selling his car, Nick Carraway walks alone to Gatsby’s abandoned house at night, erases an obscene word scrawled on the steps, and wanders to the beach, reflecting on the green light, the lost dream, and humanity’s futile struggle against time—'So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.'

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves to West Egg, Long Island, seeking purpose in the finance world and renting a modest home next to the extravagant mansion of the mysterious Jay Gatsby. Through his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom—wealthy, arrogant, and unfaithful—Nick is introduced to the glittering yet hollow world of East Egg’s elite. He also meets Jordan Baker, a cynical golf champion whose dishonesty mirrors the moral decay around them. Nick’s fascination with Gatsby begins when he witnesses him standing alone at night, arms outstretched toward a green light across the bay, symbolizing an unattainable dream. As Nick is drawn into Gatsby’s world through lavish parties and whispered rumors, he learns that Gatsby’s fortune and mansion were built solely to win back Daisy, whom he loved five years earlier before being separated by war and class.

Gatsby’s past, revealed through Jordan Baker’s recollections and his own embellished tales, traces his transformation from James Gatz, a poor North Dakota farm boy, into the self-made millionaire Jay Gatsby, shaped by his time with the wealthy Dan Cody and fueled by an obsessive idealization of Daisy. Nick agrees to arrange a secret reunion between Gatsby and Daisy, which reignites their romance, but the illusion begins to crack under Tom’s hostility. At the Plaza Hotel, tensions erupt as Tom exposes Gatsby’s criminal ties through Meyer Wolfsheim and forces Daisy to admit she once loved Tom—and still does. The confrontation shatters Gatsby’s dream, and Daisy, overwhelmed, returns to Tom. That evening, Daisy, driving Gatsby’s car, accidentally kills Myrtle Wilson, Tom’s mistress, but Gatsby takes the blame to protect her. Meanwhile, Myrtle’s widower, George Wilson, misled by Tom into believing Gatsby was both Myrtle’s lover and her killer, descends into madness, fixated on the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg as divine judgment.

After Gatsby’s death at Wilson’s hands—shot while floating in his pool—Nick is left to organize a funeral for a man whose world had no true friends. Only a handful attend: Gatsby’s father, a lonely minister, servants, the postman, and the owl-eyed man who marvels at the authenticity of Gatsby’s books. Nick’s desperate attempts to reach Daisy and Wolfsheim are met with cold indifference, and he learns Tom deliberately sent Wilson to Gatsby, knowing it would end in violence. Disillusioned by the carelessness of the wealthy, Nick realizes Gatsby’s dream was not just lost—it was doomed from the start by a society that values illusion over truth. In the final moments, Nick walks alone to Gatsby’s abandoned house, erases an obscenity on its steps, and gazes at the green light once more, reflecting on humanity’s futile struggle against time: 'So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.'
